title: Allentown Mack Sales & Service, Inc. v. National Labor Relations Board
lead: A successor dealership hears reports of declining union support and conducts a poll, leading two different Supreme Court majorities to uphold the polling standard but reject its application.

actors.name: Allentown Mack Sales & Service
actors.role: New independent dealership and successor employer.

actors.name: National Labor Relations Board
actors.role: Agency finding insufficient grounds for the employer’s poll and ordering bargaining.

actors.name: Ron Mohr, Kermit Bloch, and Dennis Marsh
actors.role: Employees whose statements were disputed evidence of reasonable uncertainty.

proceedings: The administrative law judge found polling safeguards satisfied but the required objective doubt absent.
The Board ordered bargaining and the D.C. Circuit enforced over a dissent.
The Supreme Court reversed and directed denial of enforcement while retaining the Board’s substantive standard.
limits: The poll result did not substitute for required pre-poll grounds. The historical reasonable-doubt framework and divided coalitions are described without certifying current polling or recognition rules.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent primary-source audit claimed.

sections.title: Former managers acquire the branch and hire a continuing workforce
sections.cue: Why did the new company inherit a bargaining presumption?
paragraphs: In May 1990, Mack Trucks announced sale of its Allentown, Pennsylvania factory branch. Several managers formed Allentown Mack Sales & Service, purchased the assets December 20, and operated an independent dealership. Between December 21 and January 1 they hired thirty-two of the former forty-five employees.
Local Lodge 724 of the machinists’ union had represented service and parts workers.

sources.pinpoint: Sale and Board order; 522 U.S. at 361–63, 390–91

sections.title: Employee reports prompt a refusal and an independently supervised poll
sections.cue: What evidence preceded the actual vote?
paragraphs: Before and just after the sale, employees discussed union support with the new owners. Eight interview statements arguably indicated personal opposition. Ron Mohr, a shop steward and bargaining-committee member, said the employees did not want the union and it would lose an election. Mechanic Kermit Bloch said the entire night shift of five or six opposed it. These reports were evidence of the employer’s grounds for uncertainty, not a Board-supervised determination of actual sentiment.

The union requested recognition and negotiation January 2, 1991. Allentown refused in a January 25 letter asserting good-faith doubt and announcing a secret-ballot poll. A Roman Catholic priest supervised the February 8 vote; the union lost nineteen to thirteen.

After the union filed an unfair-labor-practice charge, the administrative law judge found the dealership a successor employer, carrying a bargaining obligation and a rebuttable presumption of continuing majority support. He found compliance with polling safeguards but insufficient objective reasonable doubt beforehand. The National Labor Relations Board adopted that conclusion and ordered recognition and bargaining. A divided D.C. Circuit enforced. Successor status was not challenged in that appeal. The historical framework permitted a Board election, withdrawal of recognition, or internal poll, using the same good-faith reasonable-doubt threshold for the challenged alternatives. Allentown attacked both the threshold and what it called its covert replacement by a strict head count.

sources.pinpoint: Employee statements and proceedings; 522 U.S. at 361–64, 368–71

sections.title: Scalia finds a rational reason to restrict even a properly safeguarded poll
sections.cue: Why was polling useful if withdrawal required the same threshold?
paragraphs: Allentown argued that enough evidence to withdraw recognition should not be required merely to ask employees whether support remained. Justice Scalia’s Part II majority acknowledged awkwardness but sustained the standard. Polls can disrupt stable bargaining relationships and unsettle workers, so the Board could restrict them to situations where withdrawal might otherwise occur.

A poll could still reassure employees before withdrawal, give an employer more certainty than the minimum defense to an unfair-labor-practice charge, or prevent withdrawal followed by a prompt union election victory. It might provoke fewer charges, especially if the union won. Formal elections, though preferred by the Board, also had stronger consequences: a losing union could not seek another for a year, while losing an internal poll did not bar a Board election. Those competing considerations allowed an equal threshold without requiring the Board to select an optimal policy.

sections.title: A different majority finds reasonable uncertainty compelled by the whole record
sections.cue: How did the discounted statements matter without proving actual loss of majority?
paragraphs: Scalia’s Parts III and IV asked whether a reasonable factfinder could conclude that Allentown lacked genuine, reasonable uncertainty. Doubt did not mean firm belief in the opposite proposition. Objective evidence meant material outside subjective impressions supporting uncertainty, not conclusive proof that the union lacked a majority.

The Board credited six employees’ opposition and apparently accepted a seventh. Seven of thirty-two alone did not compel doubt, but other evidence mattered. Dennis Marsh’s complaint that representation was not worth his $35 dues might request better representation or its end; either interpretation made it relevant to uncertainty. Bloch’s report about the night shift might not establish colleagues’ actual preferences by ordinary trial standards, yet could reasonably inform an employer absent reason to think he was uninformed or dishonest.

Mohr’s report was especially significant because he was a union official positioned to observe opinion and expressed no personal hostility. The Board discounted it partly because it referred to the predecessor’s employees rather than exactly the later hires. But its successorship presumption itself relied on continuity. It could not use continuity to impose bargaining while disregarding it entirely for contrary evidence. The majority distinguished the administrative law judge’s treatment from Board language assigning the report no weight.

With seven known opponents, the other twenty-five would need to favor the union at least seventeen to eight for an overall majority. Reports of broader dissatisfaction supplied grounds to question that ratio, with no significant contrary evidence identified. Fair treatment of this circumstantial record therefore required a finding of reasonable doubt. The subsequent nineteen-to-thirteen poll did not replace the needed pre-poll showing.

sections.title: Announced standards cannot be silently replaced in the guise of factfinding
sections.cue: What remained within the Board’s policy discretion?
paragraphs: The Court did not finally decide whether earlier cases systematically used a stricter hidden test. Even repeated departures would not redefine the announced standard or justify this finding. Reasoned decisionmaking governs adjudication as well as rulemaking; covert changes in substance or proof burden confuse hearing judges, frustrate review, and conceal policy choices.

The Board could openly adopt reasonable, statutorily consistent evidentiary exclusions or substantive presumptions. But when claiming ordinary factfinding under reasonable-doubt and preponderance standards, it had to draw fair inferences. Substantial-evidence review already deferred by asking what a reasonable factfinder could find; an extra layer of deference to an eccentric evidentiary understanding would erase review. Skepticism based on lack of knowledge or motive to mislead was permissible, while precedent alone could not justify arbitrary total disregard.

sources.pinpoint: Announced and applied rule; 522 U.S. at 372–80 & n.4

sections.title: Rehnquist would also invalidate the rule, while Breyer would uphold the evidence ruling
sections.cue: What produced the unusual five-vote alignments?
paragraphs: Chief Justice Rehnquist, joined by O’Connor, Kennedy, and Thomas, agreed with reversal but would reject the threshold itself. Noncoercive polls already required purpose disclosure, notice, assurances against retaliation, secrecy, and a noncoercive atmosphere. Bargaining stability did not justify denying a neutral way to learn employee preferences. The different consequences of polling, withdrawal, and formal elections made equal thresholds irrational in his view. He also invoked serious First Amendment concerns and avoidance while declining to decide a constitutional violation.

Justice Breyer, joined by Stevens, Souter, and Ginsburg, agreed that the rule was valid but would enforce the order. He thought the application question outside the certiorari grant and Supreme Court intervention in substantial-evidence review unusually unwarranted. Objective reasonable doubt, to him, was a specialized workplace standard developed through Board experience rather than dictionary uncertainty.

Breyer emphasized that interviewees seeking reemployment might say what managers wanted, dissatisfaction did not necessarily mean rejection of representation, and Bloch named no colleagues or supporting witnesses. Mohr referred to a different service complement, could not speak for all parts employees, gave no size for the dissatisfied majority, and made what the hearing judge viewed as an offhand remark. Breyer understood that judge to have weighed it with other evidence. He saw permissible agency evidentiary guidance where the majority saw disregard and would defer.

sources.pinpoint: Separate opinions; 522 U.S. at 380–97 and Rehnquist notes

sections.title: The order loses enforcement while the stated polling rule remains valid
paragraphs: The Supreme Court reversed the D.C. Circuit and remanded with instructions to deny enforcement of the bargaining order. It did not replace reasonable doubt with unrestricted polling. Part I was unanimous. Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer joined Scalia in Part II sustaining the standard; Rehnquist, O’Connor, Kennedy, and Thomas joined him in Parts III and IV rejecting the application. Each central conclusion had five votes, with Scalia in both coalitions.

The full decision therefore separates a permissible rule from an unsupported application. Its account of the 1998 Board framework and evidentiary dispute does not certify later recognition or polling doctrine.

sources.pinpoint: Result, voting alignment, and historical scope; 522 U.S. at 360, 363–80, 388
